overview.text: A mass extinction is a geologically brief interval in which biodiversity collapses: a commonly used threshold is the loss of roughly three-quarters of species worldwide in less than about 2.8 million years. Unlike ordinary background extinctions, these crises affect many groups across Earth, and scientists recognize five major episodes within roughly the past 500 million years. They are identified chiefly from changes in the fossil record; their timing, scale and causes vary. The Permian–Triassic “Great Dying” was the most severe, while the Cretaceous–Paleogene event about 66 million years ago eliminated non-avian dinosaurs and many other organisms. Environmental upheaval—including climate shifts, volcanism or asteroid impact—can drive such losses; not every event has a fully settled explanation.

key_facts.text: A commonly used definition is the loss of about 75% of species worldwide within less than 2.8 million years.
The fossil record preserves evidence of past extinctions, including abrupt changes in which organisms appear in different layers.

The Permian–Triassic event, called the “Great Dying,” was Earth’s largest mass extinction; most marine species disappeared. Smithsonian evidence points to global warming and atmospheric changes linked to enormous Siberian eruptions.
The Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction about 66 million years ago wiped out non-avian dinosaurs and many other species; evidence supports an asteroid impact near what is now Mexico as a major cause.
Mass extinctions have different causes; examples include rapid climate change, shifting sea levels, major volcanic activity and asteroid impact.
